purpose: Map documented post-Soviet Russian/Russian-backed conflict cases in which television, radio, transmission, satellite, cable or Internet distribution infrastructure was attacked, neutralized, seized, replaced, rerouted or otherwise controlled, while preserving cases where the expected seize-and-replace pattern is not established.
scope_warning: This is a best-effort documented matrix, not a claim to have captured every tactical incident in every Russian conflict. Direct Russian action, Russian-backed/separatist action, local-authority action and unproven attribution are kept separate.

mechanism_types.A_NEUTRALIZE: Destroy or disable an opponent distribution source without immediate documented replacement.
mechanism_types.B_SEIZE_REPLACE: Take physical/logical control of a broadcast/cable distribution point and substitute aligned content.
mechanism_types.C_ROUTE_CAPTURE: Move Internet connectivity to a controlled transit/provider so users inherit another jurisdiction's filtering/surveillance environment.
mechanism_types.D_MEDIA_CONTROL_WITHOUT_TOWER_CAPTURE: Control narrative through access restrictions, state media, embeds, censorship or journalist exclusion without a documented seize-and-replace broadcast-infrastructure event.

timeline.finding: Russian air operations targeted Grozny's television tower; contemporary reporting and later military studies describe the tower being knocked out, followed by removal of the last satellite link and cuts to telephone lines.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Early example of treating mass-communication distribution as a military target; the documented mode is neutralization, not a clean same-frequency Russian-content substitution.

cases.actor: Russian Federation armed forces and federal media authorities

timeline.finding: Russian air strikes hit Grozny's television tower during the opening air campaign; Russian officials publicly showed strike footage. At the same time federal media authorities prohibited national television networks from broadcasting interviews/footage of militant leaders and military access to independent reporting was tightly controlled.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Distribution-source suppression was paired with much stronger centralized control of the domestic narrative than in the first Chechen war.

cases.actor: Abkhaz separatist forces with substantial reported Russian support; direct Russian command of the tower seizure is not established

timeline.finding: Contemporary reports say Abkhaz forces seized/controlled Sukhumi's television tower during the final battle for the city. Multiple contemporaneous accounts also reported substantial Russian military support to Abkhaz forces, but the specific tower action cannot be attributed to Russian command from the recovered public evidence.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Useful early Russian-backed conflict analog for physical importance of broadcast infrastructure, but not clean evidence of a Russian-directed information-substitution operation.

cases.actor: Russian and South Ossetian forces plus Georgian state actions on the other side

timeline.finding: Russian and South Ossetian forces restricted journalist access and detained crews in Russian-controlled/buffer areas. Reports exist of strikes or threats involving television infrastructure, but this pass did not recover sufficiently strong evidence of a Russian seize-tower-and-replace-local-signal operation comparable to Crimea/Donbas.

Georgia itself blocked Russian television and some Russian-language websites during the conflict, demonstrating that information-distribution control was contested and not uniquely Russian in this case.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Negative/alternative control: intense information warfare and press restrictions can occur without the specific physical capture-and-substitution sequence.

cases.actor: Russian occupation/local de facto authorities and armed formations under Russian control/support

timeline.finding: Major Ukrainian and independent terrestrial television signals were cut; Russian channels including NTV, Channel One, Rossiya 24, RTR, TNT and Zvezda appeared on their frequencies before the 16 March referendum. Chernomorskaya TV/radio was among the outlets removed.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Strongest rapid positive control: physical/distribution control was followed by source removal and same-medium aligned source substitution before a major political event.

cases.actor: Armed anti-government/separatist forces in a Russia-backed conflict environment

timeline.finding: OSCE reported seizure of the Sloviansk television tower, which served Sloviansk and neighboring Horlivka, Kramatorsk and Makiivka; Ukrainian channels were cut and replaced with channels from the Russian Federation.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Clear tower-first source-substitution event early in the armed phase of the Donbas conflict.

timeline.finding: OSCE reported seizure of the Donetsk Regional Television and Radio Company and regional transmission centre, with some local broadcasts replaced by Rossiya 24.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Broadcast-company plus transmission-centre capture converted control of infrastructure directly into control of source selection.

timeline.finding: OSCE reported staff of Luganskoye Kabelnoe Televideniye forced from the building and the transmission replaced by Russian 5 Kanal; UN monitoring documented broader removal of Ukrainian channels and substitution by Russian/DPR-aligned programming across the region earlier in 2014.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Extends the pattern from terrestrial towers to cable distribution and editorial coercion.

cases.actor: Russian Federation armed forces and occupation administrations

timeline.finding: U.S. State Department reporting says Russian forces took control of radio frequencies and television channels in Zaporizhzhia, Luhansk and Kherson and used existing Ukrainian broadcasting infrastructure, including major TV towers, to replace Ukrainian television/radio with Russian or DPR/LPR programming.

Melitopol mayor reported Russian forces controlled the city's television and radio towers; separate technical reporting cautioned that some early Russian television was transmitted through an external analog transmitter rather than the digital tower itself, so device-level details require care.

Ukraine's broadcast regulator reported occupation forces had seized multiple radio frequencies/TV channels across four regions; in Kherson the 99.0 MHz Armiya FM frequency was used for Radio Rossiya, and Russian television was distributed over seized multichannel capacity in multiple occupied cities.

Cloudflare measured more than twenty occupied Ukrainian networks whose routing was changed to Russian upstream providers; traffic transiting Russian networks inherited Russian restrictions, surveillance and content filtering.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Strongest modern convergence of physical broadcast replacement and Internet-path capture. Distribution control moved from spectrum/cable to AS routing while retaining the same functional outcome: external sources become harder to reach and aligned sources gain relative share.

cases.actor: Russian Federation in support of Syrian government

timeline.finding: Research documents tightly managed Russian military-media access, state-media framing and international RT/Sputnik information operations, but this pass found no comparable Russian seizure of Syrian broadcast towers followed by source substitution as a defining opening mechanism.

cases.mechanism_interpretation: Negative control demonstrating Russian conflict propaganda can be intensive without physical takeover of an opponent's broadcast distribution because the allied Syrian state already controlled substantial domestic media infrastructure.

pre_russian_federation_precursor_not_cou.finding: Soviet troops seized/attacked press and television infrastructure in Lithuania and Latvia during attempts to suppress independence movements, including the deadly assault on the Vilnius TV tower.
pre_russian_federation_precursor_not_cou.interpretation: Relevant historical precursor to the strategic value placed on mass-distribution nodes, but excluded from RF case-count because the Russian Federation did not yet exist as the acting state.

insufficient_evidence_cases.note: Do not promote to seize/replace case without a primary or strong contemporaneous source establishing the broadcast-infrastructure sequence.

evolution: 1990s: destroy or disable tower/satellite links; constrain journalists
2022+: seize frequencies/broadcast assets and also reroute Internet transit through Russian-controlled networks
cross_case_pattern.claim_limit: A recurring functional pattern does not prove one standing doctrine or centrally preplanned script across all conflicts. Each event has different actors, operational needs and evidence quality.

anti_confirmation_controls: Georgia 2008 shows high-intensity information warfare without a clean Russian tower-seize-and-replace event in recovered evidence.
Syria 2015 shows extensive Russian information operations can work through an allied state's existing media infrastructure without seizure.
Chechnya demonstrates neutralization can substitute for takeover when the objective is to deny an adversary broadcast capability.
Abkhazia 1993 must retain attribution uncertainty between Russian support and direct Russian control of specific tower actions.
Melitopol 2022 shows even apparently simple tower-seizure reports can require technical correction about which transmitter actually carried the substituted signal.
